This page goes with **Chapter 30, Introduction to Counterpoint** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/IntroductionToCounterpoint.html). Read each section there first. It builds on [Voice Leading Triads](voice-leading-triads.qmd) (the types of motion and the rules of melody in 26.1 and 26.4).

**How the page works.** Each example is drawn on a grand staff, plays when you press **Play**, and is **marked by the same checker** that marks your exercises: a green *Right*
passes it, a red *Wrong* shows what the checker says. In the exercises the given notes are greyed; type the others (`E4`, `F#4`, `Bb3`; **Up** and **Down** move a step in the key,
**Shift** a half step) and press **Check**.

Every counterpoint is written in **two voices** against a given **cantus firmus** (c.f.), a plain melody in whole notes. Here the cantus firmus is in the lower voice (counterpoint above) or in the upper voice (counterpoint below); the page says which.

## 30.1 Species counterpoint

Fux's *Gradus ad Parnassum* (1725) teaches writing by **species**: one, two, three or four notes against each whole note of the cantus firmus, in the style of Palestrina. Counterpoint is the sounding together of
melodic lines (a **contrapuntal** texture), in contrast to melody and accompaniment (**homophonic**). The book's rules are a simplified version of Fux's; the page's checker marks all five species. The invention and fugue sections at the end are described, not checked.

## 30.2 First species: note against note

Write one whole note for each note of the cantus firmus. The rules (simplified from Fux, as in the book):

- **Begin and end on a unison or octave.** Approach the final octave by **contrary motion**: one voice 7 to 8 (a half step up, with a raised leading tone in G mixolydian, D dorian and A aeolian), the other 2 to 1.
- **Every interval is a consonance**: unison, 3rd, 5th, 6th, octave and their compounds. 2nds, 4ths, 7ths and the tritone are dissonant and not allowed in first species.
- **Imperfect consonances** (3rds, 6ths) may be approached any way; **perfect consonances** (unison, 5th, octave) only by **contrary motion**, to avoid direct fifths and octaves.
- Not more than **three 3rds** (or **6ths**) in a row.
- When the cantus firmus is in the upper part, the counterpoint below uses unison, 3rd, 5th or 6th.
- Only these **leaps**: 3rds, 4ths, 5ths, ascending minor 6ths, octaves; after a leap larger than a 4th, change direction. Do not outline a tritone with two turning points. Avoid repeated notes (they hold up the flow).

## 30.3 Second species: two against one

Write **two half notes** against each whole note of the cantus firmus. (In 3/2, three half notes against a dotted whole.) The rules are the same on the downbeats, with these changes:

- **Begin** with a half note at the octave or unison on beat 1, or on beat 3 after a half rest.
- **End** with a whole note on the octave or unison. The bar before: with the cantus firmus below, a **5th then a 6th** above it (6 7 against the cantus firmus's 2); with it above, a **5th then a 3rd** below it. (Phrygian, cantus firmus above: a 6th then a 3rd.)
- The first half note of a bar is always a consonance. The second is a consonance, **or a dissonance only as a passing tone** (reached and left by step in the same direction).
- Across the barline, imperfect consonances are free, perfect ones only by contrary motion. **Do not repeat a note across a barline.** Avoid octaves on consecutive downbeats, and fifths on consecutive downbeats, unless a leap of a 4th follows the first.

## 30.4 Third species: four against one

Write **four quarter notes** to each whole note of the cantus firmus (the last bar one whole note). Begin on an octave or unison. The rules of first species still hold on the **downbeats**, plus:

- **Each downbeat is a consonance.** The other three quarters may be consonant, or dissonant only as a **passing tone** (never on beat 1) or the **cambiata**: approached by a step down from beat 1 to beat 2, left by a leap down a third, then a step up.
- Across the barline, imperfect consonances are free; a perfect one on the downbeat only by contrary motion (no direct fifths or octaves). **Do not repeat a note across a barline.**
- **The ending:** a whole note on an octave or unison. The bar before it, in scale degrees: with the cantus firmus below, **4 5 6 7** or the cambiata **2 1 6 7**; with the cantus firmus above, **7 5 6 7**. The note before the end rises a half step.

<div class="vl-spex" data-species="3" data-cfpos="lower" data-mode="D dorian" data-cf="D3 F3 E3 D3" data-cp='[["D4","F4","A4","F4"],["A4","G4","F4","A4"],["G4","A4","B4","C#5"],["D5"]]' data-expect="ok">The cantus firmus in the bass (D F E D): the downbeats are consonant, G passes between A and F, and the bar before the end is 4 5 6 7 (G A B C#) over E.</div>

## 30.5 Fourth species: suspensions

Here the counterpoint is **syncopated**: the book writes fourth species only with the cantus firmus in the lower voice.

- **Start** with a half rest, then a half note an octave above the cantus firmus. **End** with a whole note an octave above it.
- The half note on **beat 3** of every bar except the penultimate is **tied** across the barline to the first half note of the next bar. Beat 3 is always a consonance.
- If the tied note, on the next downbeat, is a **dissonance** (a 4th or a 7th above the cantus firmus) it is a **suspension** and must **resolve down by step**. Allowed in the upper part: **4-3 and 7-6**; 9-8 and 2-1 are not allowed. If the tied note is a consonance it is a **syncopation** and may go anywhere.
- The **penultimate bar** has a **7-6 suspension** (over the cantus firmus's 2, a 7th resolving to the 6th, then up to the final octave).

<div class="vl-spex" data-species="4" data-cfpos="lower" data-mode="D dorian" data-cf="D3 G3 F3 E3 D3" data-cp='[[null,"D4"],["D4","E4"],["E4","D4"],["D4","C#4"],["D4"]]' data-expect="ok">Half rest, D an octave above, then ties: D over G (a syncopation), E over F (a 7th, a suspension resolving to D), and D over E (the 7-6 that closes).</div>

<div class="vl-spex" data-species="4" data-cfpos="lower" data-mode="D dorian" data-cf="D3 G3 F3 E3 D3" data-cp='[[null,"D4"],["D4","E4"],["E4","F4"],["F4","C#4"],["D4"]]' data-expect="resolves down by step">Bar 3: the suspended E (a 7th over F) rises to F instead of falling to D.</div>

<div class="vl-spex" data-species="4" data-cfpos="lower" data-mode="D dorian" data-cf="D3 G3 F3 E3 D3" data-cp='[[null,"D4"],["D4","E4"],["G4","D4"],["D4","C#4"],["D4"]]' data-expect="Tie">Bar 3 does not begin with the E tied over from bar 2.</div>

<div class="vl-spex" data-species="4" data-cfpos="lower" data-mode="D dorian" data-cf="D3 G3 F3 E3 D3" data-cp='[[null,"D4"],["D4","E4"],["E4","D4"],["D4","D4"],["D4"]]' data-expect="7-6">The bar before the end has no 7-6 suspension.</div>

## 30.6 Fifth species: florid counterpoint

Fifth species is a **free mixture** of the first four: half notes, quarter notes and ties in one line over the cantus firmus. Hutchinson points to the opening of Lassus's *Expectatio Justorum* as an example. The checker uses what the species above establish:
the first and last rules; consonant downbeats, or a tied suspension resolving down by step; dissonance only on a **quarter note**, as a passing tone, a **neighbor tone** or a cambiata; perfect consonances on non-tied downbeats only by contrary motion; the allowed leaps.
(The neighbor tone as a dissonance and the quarter-note limit are this site's reading of "a free mixture", not rules the book states.) Type each bar as notes with lengths, `D4:2 E4:1 D4:1` (`:2` half, `:1` quarter, `r:2` a half rest); a note with no length is the bar divided evenly.

<div class="vl-spex" data-species="5" data-cfpos="lower" data-mode="D dorian" data-cf="D3 F3 E3 D3" data-cp='[["r:2","D4:2"],["A4:2","G4:1","F4:1"],["G4:2","B4:1","C#5:1"],["D5"]]' data-expect="ok">Half rest and D, then a half note A with a passing G to F, then G B C# up to the final D.</div>

<div class="vl-spex" data-species="5" data-cfpos="lower" data-mode="D dorian" data-cf="D3 G3 F3 E3 D3" data-cp='[["r:2","D4:2"],["D4:2","E4:2"],["E4:2","D4:1","D4:1"],["D4:2","C#4:2"],["D4"]]' data-expect="ok">A tied E (a 7th over F) is suspended, resolves to D, and the D is tied into the closing 7-6.</div>

<div class="vl-spex" data-species="5" data-cfpos="lower" data-mode="D dorian" data-cf="D3 F3 E3 D3" data-cp='[["r:2","D4:2"],["A4:2","G4:2"],["G4:2","B4:1","C#5:1"],["D5"]]' data-expect="only on a quarter note">Bar 2: a half-note G over F is a dissonance that lasts too long.</div>

## 30.7 Invention expositions and fugue analysis

The chapter ends with applying species to harmony: writing the four-bar **exposition** of a two-part invention on the model of Bach's C major and E minor inventions (the theme in bar 1, an octave lower in the bass in bar 2, a fifth higher in bar 3, an octave lower in bar 4, ending on a tenth: tonic in the bass, 3 above), with counterpoint that outlines the harmony of each bar
(I, then V, then back to I); and **analysing a fugue**: subject, answer (real or tonal), countersubject, episode, bridge and exposition, with motivic fragmentation. Open the Bach
fugue and invention scores in the [Analysed Scores Library](analysed-scores/view.qmd) to hear and see them. *Not checked here.*

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What the checker does and does not check
- First species: beginning, ending (contrary, 7 to 8 and 2 to 1), consonance, perfect intervals only by contrary motion, runs of 3rds and 6ths (this site reads it as three of the same kind), allowed leaps, direction change after leaps larger than a 4th, outlined tritones, repeated notes (a warning).
- Second species: the beginning on beat 1 or 3, the whole-note ending, the penultimate-bar formulas, consonant downbeats, dissonant second notes only as passing tones, no repeated note across the barline, no octaves or fifths on consecutive downbeats unless a 4th leap follows.
- Third species: consonant downbeats, passing tones and the cambiata, the 4 5 6 7 / 2 1 6 7 / 7 5 6 7 ending formulas, no repeated note across a barline. Fourth: the tie on every beat 3 but the penultimate, suspensions 4-3 and 7-6 resolving down by step (9-8 and 2-1 refused), the 7-6 before the end.
  Fifth: the common rules plus the quarter-note limit on dissonance (this site's reading of "a free mixture").
- All species: the counterpoint stays above (or below) the cantus firmus, and the note before the end rises a half step (the book gives this as 7 to 8; the checker requires it in every species, so a Phrygian cantus firmus is allowed a whole step).
- **Not checked:** consecutive leaps outlining a triad in species, the range of the counterpoint, fourth species with the cantus firmus above (the book does not write it), and the invention and fugue sections.
- The text on this page is written for the site, not copied from the book (the book is under the GNU Free Documentation License).
